keys.statement: Before setting up a heteroazeotropic column, compute and classify every azeotrope (nodes and saddles). The singular points show which profiles a column can reach at total reflux and guide the starting profile.

plain.title: Before building a heteroazeotropic column, map every azeotrope
plain.when: You set up a heteroazeotropic column (one with a decanter on top where two liquids form), and it starts far from a feasible profile.
plain.do: Compute and classify every azeotrope as a node or a saddle (points where residue curves start, end or turn). These singular points show which profiles a column can reach at total reflux and guide the starting profile.
plain.why: The mixture's topology bounds what column profiles are possible.
plain.check: In CHEPTA, check each azeotrope's temperature and composition against Kruber & Skiborowski 2022 or measured data before the first column run.

decisions.obstacle: A column started far from a feasible profile.
decisions.mechanism: The mixture topology bounds the column profiles.
decisions.expected_change: A starting point in the right distillation region.

keys.statement: Estimate the recycle and top products from an overall mass balance first: pure bottom products, a top vapour at the lowest-boiling heteroazeotrope, and a decanter splitting it into its two liquids with the solvent-lean liquid recycled.

plain.title: Guess the heteroazeotropic recycle from a mass balance, not from defaults
plain.when: The recycle composition and flow of a two-column process with a decanter are unknown.
plain.do: Solve an overall mass balance first: pure bottom products, a top vapour at the lowest-boiling heteroazeotrope, and a decanter splitting it into its two liquids, with the solvent-lean liquid recycled. Use the result as the tear guess (the recycle stream's starting value).
plain.why: The heteroazeotrope and its liquid split fix the overhead and the recycle to a first approximation.
plain.check: In CHEPTA, give this balance as the tear stream's starting value and compare the first iteration with it.

decisions.mechanism: The heteroazeotrope and its liquid split fix the overhead and recycle to a first approximation.
decisions.operation: Solve the balance, then use it as the tear guess.

keys.statement: Initialise the heteroazeotropic column with a piecewise-linear composition profile joining the lowest-boiling heteroazeotrope, the saddle of its distillation region and the bottom product. Then check phases on each stage before solving the full column.

plain.title: Start the heteroazeotropic column from a profile joining azeotrope, saddle and bottom product
plain.when: A column crossing a two-liquid region fails from a flat or constant starting profile.
plain.do: Initialise with a piecewise-linear composition profile joining the lowest-boiling heteroazeotrope, the saddle of its distillation region and the bottom product. Check the phases on each stage before solving the full column.
plain.why: At total reflux the profile follows the region's singular points, so this start lies close to the solution.
plain.check: Lab has not checked whether CHEPTA accepts a stage-by-stage starting profile; if not, start from the closest converged column.

decisions.obstacle: Flat or constant starting profiles for a column crossing a two-liquid region.
decisions.mechanism: The profile at total reflux follows the region's singular points.

keys.statement: Initialise the companion simple column by flashing its mixed feed (fresh feed plus recycle), solving the stage model with a fixed structure, and only then minimising duty; raise model complexity step by step.

plain.title: Build up the simple column step by step: flash, fixed column, then optimise
plain.when: A column model solved all at once from a poor start fails.
plain.do: Flash the mixed feed (fresh feed plus recycle) first, then solve the stage model with a fixed structure, and only then minimise duty. Raise the model's complexity one step at a time.
plain.why: Each harder sub-problem starts close to the solution of the easier one before it.
plain.check: In CHEPTA, keep each step's converged result and start the next step from it.

decisions.obstacle: A column model solved all at once from a poor start.
decisions.mechanism: Successively harder sub-problems keep each start close to the solution.
decisions.operation: Flash, then fixed-structure column, then optimisation.

keys.statement: Even one heteroazeotropic column is hard to simulate: it can have multiple steady states and its products are very sensitive to the organic reflux. Luyben's careful manual start of ethanol dehydration still ended unconverged (as cited).

plain.title: Even one heteroazeotropic column is hard: fix the organic reflux before adding the second column
plain.when: A heteroazeotropic column does not converge.
plain.do: Fix the organic reflux and recycle estimates before adding the second column. Do not read a failure as a property error alone.
plain.why: Such a column can have several steady states and its products are very sensitive to the organic reflux. Luyben's careful manual start of ethanol dehydration still ended unconverged (cited by Kruber & Skiborowski 2022).
plain.check: In CHEPTA, scan the organic reflux around the published value and record where the column converges.

decisions.mechanism: Multiple steady states and sensitivity to the organic reflux.
decisions.operation: Fix the organic reflux and recycle estimates before adding the second column.
decisions.expected_change: Expect difficulty; do not read failure as a property error alone.

keys.statement: Test phase stability on every stage: assuming vapour-liquid equilibrium only, with no second liquid, can give substantial errors in a heteroazeotropic column.

plain.title: Column with water and an organic phase gives odd profiles: allow two liquids on every stage
plain.when: A column whose liquid can split into two phases (for example water with an organic entrainer, in heteroazeotropic distillation) is computed with vapour-liquid equilibrium only, or its stage profiles look wrong.
plain.do: Test phase stability (whether a liquid would rather split into two) on every stage, and allow vapour-liquid-liquid equilibrium there. Kruber & Skiborowski 2022 cite earlier work showing that leaving out the second liquid can give substantial errors.
plain.why: On a stage that really holds two liquids, a one-liquid calculation gets the wrong equilibrium, and so the wrong compositions, flows and balance.
plain.check: In CHEPTA, set phases: "VLL" on the column and the decanter, then see which stages report two liquids and compare the decanter's two liquid compositions with those of Kruber & Skiborowski 2022.

decisions.obstacle: A stage that should split into two liquids is computed as one.
decisions.mechanism: Missing the liquid split changes the equilibrium and the balance.
decisions.operation: Use a robust stability test and allow VLLE on each stage.

keys.statement: For a gradient-based solver, a three-phase stage can be treated as a quasi vapour-liquid stage on the overall liquid, with the two-liquid split done only inside the property call. This avoids discontinuities as stages switch between one and two liquids.

plain.title: Stages switching between one and two liquids break a gradient solver: hide the split inside the property call
plain.when: A gradient-based solver meets discontinuities as stages change between one and two liquids.
plain.do: Treat each three-phase stage as a quasi vapour-liquid stage on the overall liquid, and do the two-liquid split only inside the property calculation.
plain.why: The column equations then see a smooth function, while the liquid split is still computed.
plain.check: This is a solver design choice. In CHEPTA, note which stages switch between one and two liquids when a run fails, and report it with the failure.

decisions.obstacle: Discontinuities when a stage changes between one and two liquids.
decisions.mechanism: Keeping the liquid split inside the equilibrium function hides the switch from the solver.
decisions.operation: Hide the liquid split from the column equations.
decisions.expected_change: Smooth convergence across the miscibility boundary.

keys.statement: When scanning feed composition widely, do not reuse one initialisation: the required stage numbers vary a lot, so re-initialise for each interval of feed composition.

plain.title: Scanning feed composition widely: re-initialise for each interval
plain.when: A feed-composition scan fails or gives outliers away from the first feed.
plain.do: Re-initialise the column for each interval of feed composition instead of reusing one start.
plain.why: The required stage numbers vary a lot, so a start built for one feed lies far from the solution for another.
plain.check: In CHEPTA, start each scan interval from a run converged near that feed.

decisions.obstacle: Scans that fail or give outliers away from the first feed.
decisions.mechanism: A start built for one feed lies far from the solution for another.

keys.statement: In the 1,4-dioxane and benzene case the optimisation relied on a small purge (0.8% of the feed), which the authors link to a poorer initial profile estimate.

plain.title: Heteroazeotropic recycle hard to close: allow a small purge
plain.when: The recycle through the decanter is not robust.
plain.do: Allow a small optional purge. In the 1,4-dioxane and benzene case of Kruber & Skiborowski 2022 the optimisation relied on 0.8% of the feed.
plain.why: A purge removes accumulating material and loosens the recycle. Kruber & Skiborowski 2022 link the need for it to a poorer initial profile estimate.
plain.check: In CHEPTA, record the purge flow and the product lost with it, and try to remove the purge once the loop converges.

decisions.obstacle: Reduced robustness of the recycle with the decanter.
decisions.mechanism: A purge removes accumulating material and loosens the recycle.

keys.statement: A converged design that sits well off the trend can be a poor local optimum. Small changes of the initial feed stage or total stage number removed such outliers.

plain.title: Converged design far off the trend may be a poor local optimum: nudge the feed stage or stage count
plain.when: One optimised design sits well off the trend of its neighbours.
plain.do: Change the initial feed stage or the total number of stages slightly and re-solve.
plain.why: The final fixing of stage locations can land in a worse local optimum.
plain.check: Compare the re-solved design with its neighbours.

decisions.obstacle: A solution far from the trend of its neighbours.
decisions.mechanism: The final fixing of stage locations lands in a worse local optimum.
decisions.operation: Perturb the feed stage or stage count and re-solve.
limits: Symptom purity-short is the closest controlled term; the paper's issue is a sub-optimal converged design, not a missed purity.

keys.statement: A heterogeneous azeotrope is a prerequisite for heteroazeotropic distillation and is always minimum-boiling. The usual process pairs a simple column and a heteroazeotropic column with a decanter, each giving one product as bottoms.

plain.title: Heteroazeotropic distillation needs a heterogeneous azeotrope: two columns and a decanter
plain.when: You want to break an azeotrope by heteroazeotropic distillation.
plain.do: Check that the mixture forms a heterogeneous azeotrope (one that splits into two liquids); such an azeotrope is always minimum-boiling. Then use the usual process: a simple column and a heteroazeotropic column with a decanter, each giving one product as bottoms.
plain.why: The decanter crosses the distillation boundary (a line a column profile cannot cross) by splitting the liquid.
plain.check: In CHEPTA, set phases: "VLL" and confirm that the azeotrope splits into two liquids. Alternatives: extractive or pressure-swing distillation.

decisions.mechanism: A decanter crosses the distillation boundary by liquid splitting.
decisions.operation: Two columns with a decanter on the heteroazeotropic column's overhead.

keys.statement: For dehydrating a 6 mol% ethanol broth, cyclohexane and hexane gave the same annual cost within estimate accuracy, while isooctane and toluene cost over 15% more. Solvent make-up was below 0.4% of cost.

plain.title: Ethanol dehydration: cyclohexane or hexane as entrainer; isooctane and toluene cost over 15% more
plain.when: You choose an entrainer for dehydrating a dilute ethanol broth (6 mol%) at atmospheric pressure.
plain.do: Prefer cyclohexane or hexane. Compare individually optimised processes for each solvent, not one fixed design.
plain.why: Each solvent changes the topology, the decanter split and the duties.
plain.check: Kruber & Skiborowski 2022 used NRTL with Aspen databank parameters (APV88) in their own optimisation: compare CHEPTA's azeotropes with theirs before reusing the ranking.
plain.result: Cyclohexane and hexane gave the same annual cost within estimate accuracy; isooctane and toluene cost over 15% more. Solvent make-up was below 0.4% of cost.

keys.statement: For ethanol dehydration the specific cost falls steeply up to about 20 mol% ethanol in the feed and then flattens, so pre-concentrating a dilute feed to about 20 mol% may pay. For an ethyl acetate feed already in the flat region it would not.

plain.title: Dilute ethanol: pre-concentrating to about 20 mol% may pay
plain.when: The ethanol feed to heteroazeotropic dehydration is very dilute.
plain.do: Consider a pre-concentration step near the knee of the cost curve, about 20 mol% ethanol. For a feed already in the flat region, such as the ethyl acetate case of Kruber & Skiborowski 2022, it would not pay.
plain.why: At low feed concentration most of the cost goes to handling water: specific cost falls steeply up to about 20 mol% and then flattens.
plain.check: A cited study found the saving too small for an extra column, and Kruber & Skiborowski 2022 leave it open: run your own feed-composition scan.

decisions.mechanism: Most cost goes to handling water at low feed concentration.
decisions.operation: Consider a pre-concentration step near the knee of the cost curve.
limits: A cited study found the savings too small for an extra column (ref. 27); the authors leave it open.
